issues.legal_issue: A person who obtains possession under a sale agreement with an intermediate purchaser cannot use the doctrine of part performance to protect that possession against the original owner when the owner did not contract with that person.
material_facts: The owner agreed to sell the land to an intermediate purchaser, who took possession, but no registered sale deed was executed in the intermediate purchaser’s favour.
The intermediate purchaser later agreed to sell the land to the appellant and put him in possession.
The owner had not entered into an agreement with the appellant, and the intermediate purchaser had no title or transferable interest in the land.
issues.conclusion: The appellant could not invoke the doctrine of part performance to protect his possession against the owner because there was no privity of contract between them and the intermediate purchaser had no transferable interest in the land.
issues.legal_principle: Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act provides an equitable shield for a transferee in possession against the transferor, or a person claiming under the transferor, if the statutory conditions are met; it does not create ownership or protect possession against a third party with whom the transferee has no privity. The essential conditions for the shield were set out in Shrimant Shamrao Suryavanshi v. Pralhad Bhairoba Suryavanshi (2002) 3 SCC 676. State of U.P. v. District Judge (1997) 1 SCC 496 explains that the shield operates only against the proposed transferor and does not affect ownership or bind third parties.

predicates.property_possession_dispute: The case concerns a claim to possession of property in which a party relies on an agreement and possession obtained under it.
predicates.claimant_received_possession_from_interm: The claimant received possession under an agreement made with a person who had earlier contracted with the owner.
predicates.owner_never_contracted_with_claimant: The owner did not make an agreement with the claimant concerning the property.
predicates.intermediate_purchaser_had_no_transferab: The intermediate purchaser had not obtained title or another transferable interest in the property.

issues.definition: When a possession dispute involves a claimant who received possession from an intermediate purchaser, the owner never contracted with the claimant, and the intermediate purchaser had no transferable title, the claimant cannot use part performance against the owner.

issues.legal_issue: A contract for sale of immovable property does not transfer title where the law requires a registered sale deed and no such deed is executed.
material_facts: The disputed land was immovable property valued at more than one hundred rupees.
The owner agreed to sell the land to the intermediate purchaser, but no registered sale deed was executed in that purchaser’s favour.
The intermediate purchaser later agreed to sell the land to the appellant and put him in possession.
issues.conclusion: The sale agreements did not transfer title to the intermediate purchaser or the appellant, and ownership remained with the original owner in the absence of a registered sale deed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act provides that a contract for sale does not, of itself, create an interest in or charge on immovable property, and that a sale of property valued above one hundred rupees can convey title only by registered instrument. Section 53-A protects possession in the circumstances it covers but does not confer ownership. The Court relied on State of U.P. v. District Judge (1997) 1 SCC 496 for the rule that title remains with the vendor until conveyance by registered sale deed.

predicates.immovable_property_sale_dispute: The case concerns a claim to rights in immovable property arising from an agreement to sell.
predicates.sale_contract_exists: A party agreed to sell the immovable property to another party.
predicates.registered_sale_deed_not_executed: No registered sale deed conveying the property was executed.

issues.definition: When an immovable-property sale dispute involves a sale contract but no registered sale deed, the contract does not transfer title.
